near_miss.why_not: Norse orð on the mouth is speech; Latin uerbis in the supplied facial-description passage is the parenthetic question about needing words, not words situated in the mouth. Sanskrit mata concerns opinion, not a mouth. No matched syntactic phrase.

Norse frǫgðar in the purpose phrase is intelligible as fame, but its Greek partner concerns a threatened wife. A corpus check of κλέος with ἄφθιτος found Iliad 9.413, but the Norse passage has no imperishability modifier and no demonstrated cognate fame noun. Heroic motivation alone is insufficient.

The verse context of bundle 14 has an eagle flying to hanged men; bundle 111 has eagles and ravens in an ominous dream. The supplied Greek passages lack the scavenger figure. Wider wolf searches yielded heroic animal imagery but no matching eagle/raven collocation. No cross-branch slab anchor for this figure.

near_miss.lead: Messengers bear words back to the king
near_miss.why_not: Read orþ as orð, accusative neuter plural, object of baro, preterite plural of bera. Searches for the word/bear roots found Norse repetitions but no secure Latin uerbum + fero occurrence; Homer Od. 19.565 has dreams bearing unfulfilled words, and Il. 10.337 has a spy bringing back a report. These illustrate a natural communication metaphor with lexical renewal, but the supplied Latin anchors describe fruit-bearing and flowing water, not messages.

near_miss.lead: Lie down to sleep at night
near_miss.why_not: Norse sofa and Russian спать are cognate, as are the night nouns. But Norse lagði belongs to laying decoy wood in the bed in the following context, not to lying down to sleep; the apparent three-root collocation is syntactically false. Corpus sleep/night hits repeat a natural activity and time combination; late byliny do not establish inheritance.

near_miss.why_not: Norse bróðor dóttir is a kinship description; the Armenian and Greek passages also describe relatives and marriages. Such genealogical expressions are compositionally necessary, with different relationships and predicates here, rather than a diagnostic inherited poetic collocation.

near_miss.lead: Prefer falling in battle to flight
near_miss.why_not: The Norse injunction is a specific heroic refusal of flight; the supplied Greek passages describe pursuit or diplomatic/military preparations. A Homeric flight/death search found escaping death, not the same preference formula. The contrast of cowardice and death is too broad to claim without closer wording.

Norse dag oc nott is an accusative duration pair. Homeric corpus search found Od. 10.28 and 10.80 with continuous sailing and νύκτας τε καὶ ἦμαρ. Night is cognate but the day term is renewed; uninterrupted travel naturally invites this merism. None of the supplied Greek anchors has both terms in this relation, so no slab-anchored inherited phrase is established.

Norse sætt is a feminine nominative singular agreement, bundin its passive participle, eiðum instrumental dative plural. The Sanskrit partner’s bandhu-jana means kinfolk, not an oath-bound agreement; satya-saṃdha and śāstre sthita are separate predicates. Corpus binda, bandh and oath searches yielded Norse legal bindings and Sanskrit nonmatching bonds; Greek δέω results mostly reflect need/request homographs. No cognate binding-plus-oath phrase established across the anchors.

anchors: xcl:MH_1_1_06_Yeghishe ed. page 1003 - PDF page 483 (word id 71386) (w1/2)
near_miss.why_not: The repeated kinship nouns really are cognate, but the Norse material assigns different people to genealogical roles rather than reproducing the Sanskrit or Greek coordinated parent pair. The Irish Alexander material and Armenian Christian material also require allowance for translation. Lists of relatives alone do not distinguish inherited wording from ordinary composition.

Norse inability to obtain sleep because of noise differs from Latin seeing a dream and Vedic addressing Dream and declaring knowledge of its origin. Corpus sleep/night searches found further commonplace combinations. Shared roots do not preserve a shared predicate structure or special figure.

Read ulfs as genitive singular úlfr and munn as accusative singular of munnr, governed by litar, present third singular of lita. Homeric wolf search found Il. 16.156–159: warriors compared to wolves whose cheeks are bloody after feeding on a stag. Only wolf is demonstrably cognate here; mouth/cheek, colouring, blood and the agents differ. This is a thematic comparison, and the slab Greek partner is peace negotiation, so no anchored claim.

near_miss.lead: Heart in the breast in battle
near_miss.why_not: Norse hiarta does not tremble in battle; Irish chridi, genitive singular of cride after the verbal noun of piercing, belongs to a literal fatal wound in the chest. Irish broind is the dative of brú, not the verb brúis/brúi which supplies the other mapped root. The two Irish witnesses repeat one episode pattern within one branch; courage versus anatomical penetration is not a shared figure.

The corpus supplied a close Xenophontic parallel, recorded separately as a search lead. The supplied Herodotean slab partner concerns a stormy night and provides no royal-ear figure. One cross-branch slab anchor is missing; the proverb may also reflect diffusion or independent political metaphor.

Norse myrct is an impersonal neuter predicative adjective, while the Serbian lines apostrophize night as full of darkness or mention its darkness. Corpus searches confirm ordinary Norse night-darkening expressions. Even accepting the proposed myrkr/mrak relationship, inevitable night/darkness association and late Serbian attestation do not establish a distinctive inherited collocation.

search_lead.cognate: Norse eyro (eyru, nominative neuter plural of eyra) and Greek ὦτα continue the inherited ear noun, conventionally *h₂ous-. The words for king and many are not presented as cognate.
search_lead.argument: Norse morg ero konongs eyro presents a proverb immediately fulfilled when information reaches the king. Xenophon likewise describes the king’s numerous informants as many ears, with a genitive king and plural ear noun. The exact plural political metonymy and quantification merit review, but Greek influence, proverb diffusion and independent formation must be excluded before inheritance can be argued. The Greek witnesses are outside the slab and marked excluded by the index.
